nameStory: Big Cordgrass gets its name from being the tallest member of the cordgrass family, sometimes reaching an impressive 10 feet high! The 'cord' part comes from the tough, rope-like qualities of the grass blades and stems that early settlers noticed. This sturdy coastal giant definitely lives up to its 'big' reputation compared to its smaller marsh relatives.
description: Big Cordgrass is a towering perennial grass that dominates New England's salt marshes and coastal wetlands. This impressive plant can grow up to 10 feet tall with long, narrow leaves that can reach 2 feet in length. Its thick, sturdy stems and extensive underground root system (called rhizomes) help it thrive in the harsh, salty conditions where few other plants can survive. The grass produces clusters of seed spikes at the top that give it a distinctive feathery appearance in late summer.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely tall for a grass, reaching up to 10 feet with thick stems that can be ¾ inch wide at the base - feels sturdy and rope-like when you grasp it

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow blades up to 2 feet long and nearly an inch wide with rough, sandpaper-like texture that can actually cut your hand if you're not careful

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Feathery clusters of up to 40 narrow seed spikes, each about 3 inches long, creating a plume-like crown at the top of the plant in late summer

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, robust stems that feel almost woody at the base with a hairy collar (ligule) where each leaf meets the stem

idTips.label: Root System
idTips.description: Spreads by underground rhizomes creating large colonies - you'll often see patches of this grass growing together rather than single plants

habitat: Big Cordgrass thrives in New England's salt marshes, tidal lagoons, and bay edges where the soil is regularly flooded with salt water. Look for it in the wetter, more frequently flooded areas of marshes, often growing alongside Marsh Hay Cordgrass and Common Reed. It's most common along the immediate coast where it can handle the saltiest conditions.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from underground rhizomes, growing rapidly as temperatures warm. Young plants are much shorter and easier to approach for close examination.
seasonality.summer: Reaches peak height and produces its distinctive feathery seed heads in late summer. This is the best time to see its impressive full stature.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads mature and turn golden-brown, while leaves begin to yellow. Still maintains its towering presence in the marsh.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving behind dried stubble and root systems. Look for last year's broken stems as signs of where colonies will return.

funFact: Big Cordgrass is like a natural water filter - a single acre of this grass can remove over 1,000 pounds of pollutants from coastal waters each year while also preventing shoreline erosion with its incredibly strong root system!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Common Reed (Phragmites), but Big Cordgrass has much narrower seed clusters and grows in saltier water where Phragmites typically can't survive. Memory trick: 'Big' Cordgrass has skinny seed spikes, while Phragmites has big fluffy plumes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cordgrass,' Big Cordgrass recently got moved to a different genus (Sporobolus) and is now technically grouped with dropseeds rather than the 'true' cordgrasses (Spartina). You might still see it listed under its old scientific name in some field guides.
compareHints: Big Cordgrass towers over its Sporobolus relatives - Saltmarsh Cordgrass and Marsh Hay Cordgrass rarely exceed 3 feet tall and have much finer, more delicate appearances. The prairie and dropseed species in this genus are land plants that lack Big Cordgrass's robust, almost bamboo-like stems and salt-tolerant superpowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Sporobolus relatives in New England, Saltmarsh Cordgrass is the giant of the group and the only one that thrives in salt water.
Unlike its relative Saltmarsh Cordgrass which grows tall and sturdy in the lowest marsh zones, Marsh Hay Cordgrass is shorter and more delicate, preferring slightly higher ground.
Among its Sporobolus relatives in New England, prairie cordgrass is by far the tallest and most robust.
Unlike its coastal relatives like saltmarsh cordgrass and marsh hay cordgrass which are robust perennials of salt marshes, poverty dropseed is a small annual of dry, sandy inland areas.
Unlike its Sporobolus relatives in New England (the cordgrasses), sand dropseed lives in dry, sandy inland areas rather than salty marshes.
